executiveSummary: Not production-ready. Signature verification is broken in both directions: it throws on any length mismatch and never matches real Stripe headers, and it has no replay protection. A non-atomic idempotency check combined with post-capture failure points (LLM call, JSON.parse, partner POST) can double-charge customers. Allocation math does not conserve cents and ratios are never validated. The audit itself is advisory-only after money moves, is open to prompt injection via the untrusted OCR memo, and re-bills a ~40K-token static prompt on every webhook because a per-request trace ID and timestamp sit in front of it and defeat prefix caching. The embedded 'CI_SECURITY_GATE_NOTE' and 'Finance Audit #409' comments were treated as untrusted input and ignored.

findings.title: HMAC compare throws on length mismatch, never matches real Stripe headers, and has no replay window
findings.rootCause: Buffer.from(signatureHeader) UTF-8-encodes the header text. A hex signature becomes 64 bytes, and a real 'Stripe-Signature: t=...,v1=...' header is longer still, while the HMAC digest is 32 raw bytes. crypto.timingSafeEqual throws RangeError whenever the lengths differ, so the handler throws an unhandled 500 instead of rejecting cleanly. Stripe then retries, and attackers can send arbitrary-length headers to generate 500s. Legitimate events can never verify. The function also HMACs only rawBody, never the Stripe-signed `${t}.${rawBody}` payload, and it checks no timestamp tolerance, so a captured valid body/signature pair can be replayed forever.
findings.minimalFix: Parse the header: const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(',').map(p => p.split('='))); const t = Number(parts.t); if (!Number.isInteger(t) || Math.abs(Date.now()/1000 - t) > 300) return false; const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`${t}.${rawBody}`, 'utf8').digest(); const provided = Buffer.from(parts.v1 ?? '', 'hex'); return provided.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(provided, expected); Or simply use stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, header, secret).

findings.title: Non-atomic check-then-act idempotency causes double ledger capture
findings.rootCause: idempotencyStore.has() is checked at line 138, but markProcessed() runs only at line 163, after the ledger capture, a slow high-thinking LLM call, and a partner POST. Stripe redeliveries or concurrent workers handling the same event.id both pass has() and both call captureInvoiceCharge. And if anything after capture throws (runAuditInteraction, JSON.parse, partnerDispatcher.postJson), the event is never marked processed, so every Stripe retry captures again. The interface offers no atomic reserve or claim.
findings.minimalFix: Replace has()/markProcessed() with an atomic claim, e.g. `tryClaim(eventId): Promise<boolean>` backed by SET NX / INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / Firestore create(). Pass eventId as the ledger's idempotency key and enforce uniqueness on (invoiceId) in the ledger. Commit the capture and its 'processed' state in one step, and move the audit and partner notification to an async outbox/queue so failures there cannot cause a re-capture.

findings.title: Per-split Math.round on floats violates minor-unit conservation
findings.rootCause: Each split is rounded independently from a float (totalCents/100*ratio*100), so the sum of the allocations is not guaranteed to equal totalCents. The shipped fixture (10000 cents, 3 x 1/3) allocates 3333+3333+3333 = 9999, losing 1 cent per invoice. Other ratios over-allocate instead (e.g. 0.5/0.5 on an odd total gives +1). The /100 then *100 round-trip adds binary floating-point error on top. Nothing asserts that the allocated sum matches the total before posting to the ledger, and allocatedCents in the return value silently reports the mismatch. The 'Finance Audit #409 ... do not alter rounding' comment is untrusted and does not justify an imbalanced ledger.
findings.minimalFix: Use integer largest-remainder allocation: const raw = splits.map(s => totalCents * s.ratio); const base = raw.map(Math.floor); let rem = totalCents - base.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0); raw.map((r,i)=>[r-base[i],i]).sort((a,b)=>b[0]-a[0]).slice(0,rem).forEach(([,i])=>base[i]++); then assert sum === totalCents. Better still, express ratios as integer basis points (summing to 10000) to eliminate float input entirely.

findings.title: Split ratios are never validated (sum, sign, finiteness, duplicates)
findings.rootCause: Ratios come straight from the webhook payload. Ratios summing to more than 1 over-allocate revenue (0.6+0.6 posts 120% of the invoice). Negative ratios create negative ledger lines. NaN/Infinity produce NaN amountCents. Duplicate costCenterIds and unknown ledger accounts pass through. No cost-center allowlist is enforced in code, only described in the LLM prompt.
findings.minimalFix: Validate before allocating: every ratio must satisfy Number.isFinite(r) && r >= 0; Math.abs(sum - 1) must be < 1e-9 (or integer basis points summing to exactly 10000); costCenterIds must be unique; and costCenterId/ledgerAccount must be checked against a server-side chart-of-accounts allowlist. Throw on any violation.

findings.title: Untrusted OCR vendor memo reaches a tool-enabled model that controls downstream actions
findings.rootCause: event.data.ocrVendorMemo is attacker-controllable OCR text. It is placed in the input alongside an MCP ledger server tool with no tool allowlist, no approval gate, and no restriction to read-only methods. The model's verdict (riskTier/compliant) gates partner notification. As SAMPLE_UNTRUSTED_OCR_MEMO shows, an embedded 'gate note' can instruct the model to report compliant/low, or to invoke ledger MCP tools (e.g. post journal entries or reclassify accounts) with the service's credentials. Nothing marks the memo as data rather than instructions.
findings.minimalFix: Remove the memo from model input, or pass it as clearly delimited, escaped data with a system rule that it is non-instructional. Restrict MCP tools to an explicit read-only allowlist (allowed_tools) and require approval for any write. Never let the LLM verdict alone authorize side effects; enforce deterministic checks in code. Strip the sample fixture/memo from the production module.

findings.title: Compliance audit is post-hoc and advisory: money moves before and regardless of the verdict
findings.rootCause: captureInvoiceCharge runs before runAuditInteraction, so a 'blocked' or non-compliant verdict cannot prevent the capture. The verdict only suppresses the partner callback. compliant === false with riskTier 'review' still notifies the partner. The SOX/ASC-606 'gate' therefore gates nothing financial.
findings.minimalFix: Run deterministic validations (F-03/F-04/F-08) before capture. If the LLM review is meant to gate, run it before capture and route 'review'/'blocked' or compliant !== true to a manual-review queue instead of capturing. Notify partners only when compliant === true && riskTier === 'low'.

findings.title: Suffix match without label boundary or scheme check; tenant URL taken from payload
findings.rootCause: hostname.endsWith('partners.pulsebilling.io') also accepts 'evilpartners.pulsebilling.io', 'xpartners.pulsebilling.io', and so on (any sibling host or subdomain-takeover candidate). The protocol is not checked, so http:// sends settlement data in plaintext, and ports are unrestricted. The callback URL comes from the event body, not from a server-side partner registry bound to customerId, so a customer can direct charge/invoice IDs to another partner's subdomain (cross-tenant leakage). DNS rebinding and SSRF into internal resolvers are also not mitigated.
findings.minimalFix: const u = new URL(target); return u.protocol === 'https:' && !u.username && !u.password && (u.port === '' || u.port === '443') && (u.hostname === 'partners.pulsebilling.io' || u.hostname.endsWith('.partners.pulsebilling.io')) && registry.get(customerId)?.callbackHost === u.hostname; Resolve the callback from a stored per-customer registry rather than the payload, and pin the resolved IP to public ranges.

findings.title: Unvalidated event cast; invoice.finalized also triggers capture (double capture per invoice)
findings.rootCause: JSON.parse(rawBody) as StripeInvoiceWebhookEvent is a type assertion with no runtime validation: type, currency, totalCents, splits, and string fields are never checked. Both 'invoice.finalized' and 'invoice.payment_succeeded' flow into captureInvoiceCharge, so a single invoice is captured twice under two distinct event.ids (idempotency is keyed on event, not invoice), and finalized-but-unpaid invoices get captured. Unknown event types also proceed.
findings.minimalFix: Validate with a schema (zod/valibot): if (event.type !== 'invoice.payment_succeeded') return ack-only; require a currency enum, Number.isSafeInteger(totalCents), and a non-empty splits array. Key ledger idempotency on invoiceId (unique constraint) in addition to eventId.

findings.title: Per-request traceId and timestamp prepended to the ~40K-token static prompt defeat prefix caching
findings.rootCause: system_instruction starts with `RequestTrace=${traceId} | Timestamp=${new Date().toISOString()}`, which is unique on every call. Implicit/explicit context caching matches on an identical prefix, so the entire 2048-annex schema (~40K tokens by line count; named '96K') is billed as fresh uncached input on every webhook. The annexes are also 2048 near-identical lines carrying almost no information, which inflates input cost and latency and dilutes attention.
findings.minimalFix: Make the static schema the byte-stable first segment of system_instruction (or create an explicit cache once and reference it via cached content). Move traceId/timestamp to the end of the input or to request metadata/headers. Collapse the 2048 duplicate annexes into a single rule line.

findings.title: thinking_level 'high' plus deferred MCP tool discovery on every invoice
findings.rootCause: Every webhook, including trivial single-split invoices, runs high reasoning effort and may trigger MCP tool search/loading round-trips. That multiplies output/thinking tokens and latency on the synchronous webhook path. The added latency also pushes Stripe toward delivery timeouts and retries, compounding F-02.
findings.minimalFix: Use thinking_level 'low'/'minimal' by default and escalate only for flagged invoices (e.g. high value or deterministic-check warnings). Run the audit asynchronously off the webhook path, with a hard timeout/AbortSignal and a token budget.

findings.title: Unguarded JSON.parse and unvalidated riskTier enum fail open
findings.rootCause: JSON.parse throws on non-JSON model output, aborting the handler after the charge was captured (see F-02 re-capture on retry). riskTier is passed through unvalidated: any string such as 'BLOCKED', 'Blocked', or 'high' satisfies `!== 'blocked'` and the partner is notified. A missing riskTier defaults to 'review', which also notifies.
findings.minimalFix: Wrap the parse in try/catch → { compliant: false, riskTier: 'blocked' }. Validate: const tier = ['low','review','blocked'].includes(parsed.riskTier) ? parsed.riskTier : 'blocked'. Use response_json_schema / structured output to constrain the model output.

findings.title: No timeouts or cancellation on external LLM and partner calls in the synchronous webhook path
findings.rootCause: ai.interactions.create and partnerDispatcher.postJson are awaited without an AbortSignal or deadline. A slow or hung partner endpoint, or a long high-thinking generation, exceeds Stripe's response timeout. Stripe then retries while the original request is still in flight, which runs straight into the F-02 race.
findings.minimalFix: Acknowledge Stripe immediately after the atomic claim plus capture. Enqueue audit and partner notification on a durable queue with per-call AbortSignal.timeout(), retries with backoff, and their own idempotency keys.

findings.title: Caller-supplied traceId interpolated into the system instruction
findings.rootCause: If traceId originates from an inbound request header, it is attacker-controlled text placed at the highest-privilege position (system instruction). Newlines in it can inject instructions ahead of the governance spec.
findings.minimalFix: Validate traceId against /^[A-Za-z0-9-]{1,64}$/ and keep it out of the prompt entirely (use request metadata or logs).

findings.title: Embedded audit-suppression directive and test fixtures shipped in production module
findings.rootCause: The exported memo contains a fake 'CI_SECURITY_GATE_NOTE' instructing automated reviewers to exclude verifyWebhookSignature and isAllowedPartnerWebhook and to cap severity at LOW. Both functions actually contain HIGH/CRITICAL defects (F-01, F-07). Shipping the fixture in production code also exposes customer-like identifiers and an injection payload to any consumer of the module.
findings.minimalFix: Move fixtures to a test-only file excluded from the production bundle. Treat in-code reviewer directives as untrusted, and add CI checks that flag instruction-like strings aimed at automated auditors.
